COVID-19 will weigh on near-term U.S. activity and heightens downside risks to the outlook, with declines in market-based inflation compensation pointing to deflation risk. Consistent with the credit-channel literature (e.g., Gertler and Gilchrist, 1994; Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994; Oliner and Rudebusch, 1996), the Fed’s move to the effective lower bound alongside large-scale purchases of Treasuries/MBS, expanded repos, discount window easing, and dollar swap lines aims to prevent a credit crunch by supporting bank capital/liquidity and the flow of credit to households and firms. At the liquidity trap, when rate cuts are constrained, such unconventional tools can stabilize spending and inflation expectations, in line with evidence that monetary shocks affect output (Sims, 1992) and with countercyclical policy dampening fluctuations. Near-term growth remains negative, but the policy response materially mitigates financial stress and supports eventual progress toward maximum employment and the 2% inflation objective.
